13370: "Realize" has three distinct meanings. All three share a common thread: something moves from being hidden, potential, or imaginary into being clear, actual, or concrete.
Meaning 1: To suddenly become aware of something

This is the most common meaning in everyday speech. When you "realize" something, a moment happens in your mind where something that was previously unclear, unnoticed, or unknown suddenly becomes clear to you.

  • I realized I had left my phone at home.
  • She realized she was being lied to.
  • He slowly realized that no one was coming.

The defining quality of this meaning is that there is a moment of recognition — something "clicks" inside you. Before this moment, you didn't know, or didn't fully grasp something. After it, you do.

This meaning is almost always personal and situational. You use it when you come to understand something about your own situation, feelings, or surroundings — not just general facts about the world. For example, you would not typically say "I realized that the sun rises in the east" because that is general knowledge everyone simply learns. But you would say "I realized that the window I had kept open all night was the reason I was cold" — because that's a personal discovery you arrived at through a moment of awareness.

Important nuances within this meaning:

a) Realizing something you had wrong:
"I realized I had completely misunderstood her instructions."
This is a very natural fit for "realize" — discovering that what you believed was mistaken.

b) Realizing the true significance of something:
"Only years later did I realize how much she had done for me."
Here, you may have known the basic facts all along. But "realize" captures the moment you fully grasped their depth, weight, or importance — something beyond just knowing.

c) Realizing an emotion:
"Midway through the conversation, I realized I was nervous."
The emotion was already there. But your conscious recognition of it came as a separate event — and that recognition is what "realize" describes.

d) "Suddenly realized" vs. "slowly realized":
Both are correct. "Suddenly realized" captures a sharp, quick mental click — the classic image of a lightbulb switching on. "Slowly realized" means understanding grew gradually over time, but "realize" still marks the point of arrival — the moment it became fully clear.

How "realize" differs from similar words:

Know: To know something means you already have that information — it is in your possession. "I know she is honest." To realize something means you come to know it. It describes the journey arriving at knowledge, not the knowledge itself. "I realized she was honest only after I saw how she handled a difficult situation."

Understand: "Understand" is primarily about grasping logic, meaning, or concepts. "I understand how electricity works." "Realize" is more about personal awareness — a recognition of a fact, situation, or feeling that concerns you specifically.

Notice: To notice something is to perceive it with your senses or attention. "I noticed a strange sound." To realize is more internal — a mental recognition, often of meaning or implication. You might notice that a friend is being quiet, and then realize that she is upset with you. Notice is often the doorway; realize is often what happens next.
Meaning 2: To achieve or bring something into reality

In this meaning, "realize" means to make something actual that was previously only a dream, ambition, plan, or potential. When you "realize a dream," you don't just dream it — you actually achieve it. You bring it from the world of imagination into the world of fact.

  • She realized her dream of becoming a doctor. (She actually became one.)
  • He worked his whole life to realize his potential. (To actually bring out what he was capable of.)
  • The project was finally realized after years of planning. (It was actually built and completed.)
  • The city council's vision was realized when the park finally opened.

The key word here is finally — you will often notice it used with "realize" in this meaning, because the whole point is that something which was waiting in the future (a hope, a plan, a possibility) has now actually happened.

This meaning is very common in formal writing, motivational speech, and discussions of goals, ambitions, and projects. It is particularly paired with words like: dream, ambition, goal, potential, vision, plan, hope.

A useful way to understand this meaning: potential is not the same as reality. A talented person who never tries has potential, not achievement. When they actually do it — when they accomplish what they were capable of — that is when potential is "realized."
Meaning 3: To obtain or earn money from something (financial)

This is a formal, specialized meaning used in business, finance, and commerce. When you "realize" a profit, gain, or sum of money, you actually receive or obtain that money — usually through a sale or transaction.

  • The auction realized over two million dollars. (The auction brought in / earned that amount.)
  • He realized a significant profit from selling his shares. (He actually received the profit when the sale was completed.)
  • She realized $80,000 from the sale of her apartment.

The core idea here is conversion — you had something of potential value (a house, shares, a painting, an investment), and by completing a transaction, you converted that potential into actual money in hand. Until you sell, a gain exists only "on paper." When you realize it, the money is real and in your possession.

This is also why you can "realize a loss" — if you sell something for less than you paid, you have converted a paper loss into an actual one.
How all three meanings are connected

Once you see the pattern, the word makes complete sense:

  • Meaning 1 — A hidden truth becomes consciously known. (Something abstract → something clear)
  • Meaning 2 — A dream or goal becomes actual. (Something potential → something real)
  • Meaning 3 — A paper value becomes actual money. (Something potential → something obtained)

In every case, "realize" describes the movement of something crossing from one state — hidden, imagined, or possible — into another state — known, achieved, or received. The word always captures that crossing moment.

"Realize" is not used to make someone else aware. In Meaning 1, you can only "realize" something yourself. You cannot say "She realized him his mistake" — that is wrong. You would say "She made him realize his mistake" or "She helped him realize what had gone wrong."

"Realize" works in the passive voice (mostly for Meaning 2): "His vision was never realized." This means: what he had hoped or planned for was never actually achieved.

"Realize" in Meaning 1 is almost always followed by "that" or a noun:

  • I realized that I was late. ✓
  • I realized my mistake. ✓
  • I realized what was happening. ✓
13371:
A realm is a defined space or domain — an area that "belongs to" or is governed by something or someone. Think of it as a complete world unto itself, with its own rules, contents, and boundaries (even if those boundaries are invisible or imaginary).

The word has two major lives: one literal and historical, one figurative and modern. Both are widely used, and understanding both is key.

In its oldest and most concrete sense, a realm is a kingdom — a territory ruled by a king or queen. It is the land, the people, and everything within the sovereign's rule.

"The king rode to the far corners of the realm."
"No enemy had ever crossed into the realm."

In this sense, realm is essentially a more formal, grand-sounding word for "kingdom." You'll encounter this meaning in historical texts, old literature, legal documents, and fantasy stories with kings and queens. It carries a serious, weighty, almost majestic tone.

A well-known phrase that captures this use is "defender of the realm" — a title meaning someone who protects the kingdom.
2. The Figurative Meaning — A Field or Domain of Something

This is the far more common use in modern English. Here, a realm is not a physical territory at all. Instead, it refers to a particular area, field, or sphere of life, thought, experience, or activity.

You can think of it this way: just as a kingdom is a space where a king has authority, a "realm" in this sense is a space where a certain subject, idea, or force holds sway.

"She was an expert in the realm of medicine."
"That idea belongs in the realm of pure fantasy."
"The discovery opened up an entirely new realm of possibilities."

Here are some of the most common "realms" people refer to:

  • The realm of science — everything that science covers and deals with
  • The realm of politics — the world of political life and power
  • The realm of imagination — the space of imagined, invented, or fictional things
  • The realm of emotion — the inner world of feelings
  • The spiritual realm — the domain of spirits, souls, or the divine (as opposed to the physical world)
  • The realm of possibility — the space of things that can actually happen

When someone says something is "within the realm of possibility," they mean it is genuinely possible — it exists inside that domain. And when something is "beyond the realm of possibility" or "outside the realm of..." — it simply cannot happen, or does not belong there.

"Finishing the project in one day is not within the realm of possibility."
"His behaviour was beyond the realm of acceptable conduct."

In games, novels, and fantasy worlds, a realm is often used to describe a distinct world, dimension, or plane of existence — sometimes magical, sometimes dark, sometimes divine.

"The hero travelled to a hidden realm beneath the mountains."
"The spirit was banished to another realm."

This use blends both meanings above — it is like a kingdom (a ruled, defined territory), but it is also an entire world of its own kind.

One very important thing to understand about realm is its register — that is, the level of formality and grandeur it carries.

"Realm" sounds elevated, formal, and slightly literary. It is more impressive-sounding than plain alternatives like "area," "field," or "world." This is why writers, speakers, and journalists reach for it when they want to describe something with a sense of scale, importance, or completeness.

Compare these:

  • "She works in the area of psychology." — plain, neutral
  • "She works in the realm of psychology." — feels broader, grander, more encompassing

Neither is wrong, but realm implies you are talking about the whole vast domain of that subject, not just a corner of it.

Because of this tone, you'll rarely hear "realm" in very casual speech. You're far more likely to see it in writing, formal talks, journalism, literature, or any context where someone wants to speak with a little weight and elegance.

UseWhat it meansExample
LiteralA physical kingdom ruled by a monarch"The army defended the realm."
FigurativeA field, domain, or sphere of something abstract"In the realm of science, this is groundbreaking."
Fantasy/FictionA distinct world or dimension"A portal to another realm opened."

If you can replace "realm" with "the world of," "the domain of," or "the kingdom of" and still make sense — you're using it correctly.

"The realm of art" = "The world of art" ✓
"The realm of England" = "The kingdom of England" ✓
"Beyond the realm of reason" = "Beyond the domain of reason" ✓

That's the word realm — in full.
13372: Realpolitik is the practice of making political decisions based entirely on practical considerations — especially power and national self-interest — rather than on moral values, ideals, or principles.

Most people like to think that governments make decisions based on values: defending freedom, protecting human rights, standing up for what is right. Realpolitik says: that's not how the real world actually works, and leaders who govern that way are being naive. What actually drives political decisions — or what should drive them, according to this approach — is cold, unsentimental calculation. What makes us stronger? What keeps us secure? What gives us more power and influence? Those questions come first. Everything else is secondary.

The word is used most often in international relations and foreign policy, though it can apply to domestic politics as well. It refers to a whole style of thinking and governing, not just a single decision.

Imagine you run a small business. An idealist business owner says, "I will only work with suppliers who share my values — ethical labor practices, environmental responsibility, honesty." A realpolitik business owner says, "I will work with whoever helps my business survive and grow. Values are nice, but the bottom line comes first."

Now apply that logic to a nation on the world stage, replace "bottom line" with "national interest and power," and you have realpolitik.
What it looks like in practice

The clearest example in modern history is President Nixon's decision to open diplomatic relations with Communist China in 1972. For years, the United States had refused to formally recognize China on ideological grounds — China was communist, authoritarian, and an adversary. But Nixon and his advisor Henry Kissinger, one of the most famous practitioners of realpolitik, recognized something: befriending China would drive a wedge between China and the Soviet Union, weakening America's biggest rival in one move. So they did it. No moral approval of China's government was implied. No ideological conversion happened. It was purely strategic. That is textbook realpolitik.

Another example: many democratic countries continue to maintain strong trade and diplomatic relationships with authoritarian governments, not because they approve of how those governments treat their people, but because the economic and security benefits are too valuable to walk away from. Realpolitik says the nation's practical interests outweigh moral objections.

The 19th-century German statesman Otto von Bismarck is considered the original master of realpolitik. He built a unified Germany through a series of carefully calculated wars, alliances, and betrayals — all engineered to maximize Prussian and then German power, with morality barely entering the picture.

To understand realpolitik sharply, it helps to see what it stands against.

Political idealism holds that foreign policy should be guided by moral values — human rights, justice, democracy, international law. An idealist leader might refuse to ally with a brutal dictator even if it would be strategically brilliant. They would say: some things are more important than advantage.

A realpolitik thinker sees this as dangerously naive. In their view, the world is a competitive arena of self-interested states, and leaders who let sentiment and ideology cloud their judgment are putting their country at risk. Principles are a luxury that powerful nations might occasionally afford, but never at the cost of real strategic interests.

In the real world, most foreign policy is a mixture of both approaches. But realpolitik is the label for the end of that spectrum closest to pure, unsentimental pragmatism.

It is not simply being selfish or reckless. In fact, realpolitik often demands careful, long-term strategic patience — it just strips away emotional or moral reasoning from that calculation. A realpolitik thinker can be perfectly pleasant in negotiation; they just aren't guided by feelings or ethics when it comes to outcomes.

It is also not the same as being evil or cruel. A leader practicing realpolitik isn't necessarily a villain — they are simply someone who has decided that results and state power take precedence over abstract principles. Whether you think that makes them admirable or troubling depends on your own values.

It is not the same as opportunism or chaos. Realpolitik is actually quite structured in its logic: it has a clear priority (national interest and power), a clear method (realistic assessment of the situation), and a clear goal (security, influence, stability).

Realpolitik has genuine, serious critics, and their arguments deserve to be understood.

Critics say that realpolitik enables and rewards dictators, because powerful nations will side with brutal governments as long as it's strategically useful. It normalizes turning a blind eye to human suffering when it's inconvenient to notice. When a democracy shakes hands with an autocrat for strategic gain, it arguably corrodes its own moral authority and sends a message that values are negotiable. Critics also argue that a world run purely on realpolitik logic is a world where might makes right, and weaker nations or oppressed populations have no one to appeal to.

Defenders of realpolitik argue that it produces more stable, predictable outcomes than idealism does. They point out that morality-driven foreign policy has led to costly, destabilizing adventures — wars fought to "spread democracy" or "remove evil regimes" that left chaos behind. Pragmatic engagement, they argue, creates more durable peace precisely because it is based on real interests rather than shifting moral fashions. They also argue that realpolitik is simply honest — it describes how the world actually works, and pretending otherwise is dangerous.

Neither side has fully won this argument. It remains one of the central debates in political philosophy and international relations to this day.

Realpolitik is a noun. It has no plural form — you don't say "realpolitiks." It is often used without an article, like a concept rather than a countable thing:

"Her foreign policy was driven by realpolitik, not sentiment."
"Critics accused the administration of realpolitik, saying it ignored the humanitarian crisis for the sake of oil."
"Realpolitik, not idealism, shaped the Cold War's strangest alliances."

In everyday usage, the word often carries a slightly cynical or critical tone — implying that someone has quietly abandoned their stated principles in favor of cold self-interest. In academic or diplomatic circles, however, it can be used in a more neutral or even admiring way, to describe shrewd, clear-eyed statecraft. Context usually tells you which is meant.
Realpolitik means: in politics, power and practical self-interest come first — ideals and morality come second, if at all.
13373: The word ream has two closely related uses — one very specific and precise, and one loose and figurative. Both flow from the same core idea: a large, counted quantity of something.
Meaning 1: A measured unit of paper

A ream is a standard unit used to measure and sell paper. One ream equals 500 sheets of paper. When you walk into a stationery shop and buy a pack of printer paper, that pack almost always contains one ream — 500 sheets bundled together.

This is a precise, technical measurement, the same way "a dozen" means exactly 12, or "a gross" means exactly 144. A ream means exactly 500.

Examples:

  • "I need to buy two reams of paper for the office printer."
  • "The box contains five reams, so there are 2,500 sheets in total."
  • "She printed so many documents that she went through an entire ream in one afternoon."

A small but important accuracy note: Historically, a ream was not always 500 sheets. For centuries, a ream meant 480 sheets. There was also a "short ream" of 472 sheets and a "long ream" of 516 sheets, depending on the industry and country. These older counts existed because printers needed a few spare sheets to account for errors during printing. Over time, as printing became more precise and standardized, the count settled on 500 sheets, which is what a ream means in virtually all modern, everyday contexts. If you ever come across very old books or documents talking about paper quantities, keep this in mind.
Meaning 2: A large, unspecified amount (informal, almost always plural)

In informal everyday language, reams (note: almost always used in the plural) means a very large amount of something — especially writing, text, information, or paperwork. It's a way of saying "a huge pile" or "an overwhelming quantity."

This meaning is a natural extension of the first — if one ream is already 500 sheets, then "reams of something" suggests mountains of it.

Examples:

  • "The investigation produced reams of documents."
    (= an enormous amount of paperwork)
  • "She wrote reams and reams of notes during the lecture."
    (= she wrote a huge, almost excessive amount)
  • "I've read through reams of research on this topic and still can't find a clear answer."
    (= vast quantities of research material)
  • "The new law generated reams of criticism from experts."
    (= a great deal of written criticism)

In this second sense, "reams" is used just like you might say "tons of," "heaps of," or "loads of." It's informal, expressive, and slightly exaggerated for effect. Nobody is literally counting 500 sheets — it just means a lot.

The link between them is intuitive. Because a ream of paper (500 sheets) already feels like a lot — it's a hefty, weighty pack — the word naturally evolved to describe any large, somewhat overwhelming quantity, especially of written or printed material. When someone says there are "reams of evidence," they're painting a picture of a towering stack of papers.

• At a stationery store or office supply shop: "A4 paper, 80 GSM, 1 ream (500 sheets)" — this is printed right on the packaging.
  • In journalism, legal writing, and academia: Writers use "reams of" to describe large bodies of documents, data, or text.
  • In literature: Authors use it for vivid, slightly dramatic effect — "he left behind reams of unpublished manuscripts."

Ream (specific)Exactly 500 sheets of paper
Reams (informal)A very large, overwhelming amount of something (especially text or paperwork)

In short: if someone hands you a ream of paper, count yourself lucky — that's 500 sheets. And if someone says there are "reams" of a problem, brace yourself — there's a lot to deal with.
13374:
To reap means to cut and collect a crop — grains like wheat, barley, or rice — when it is ready to be harvested. Farmers reap their fields after months of growing. This is the original, literal meaning.

But in everyday modern language, "reap" is used far more often in a figurative sense: to receive or obtain something as a direct result of your own actions or efforts. The result can be good or bad.

The word carries a powerful underlying idea: the result is connected to what you did before. Just like a farmer who plants seeds and later cuts down the grown crop, a person "reaps" the outcome of their earlier choices, work, or behavior.

This is why the most famous phrase using this word is:

"You reap what you sow."

"Sow" means to plant seeds. So the phrase means: what you put in is what you get out. If you plant wheat, you harvest wheat — not rice. If you work hard, you gain rewards. If you act dishonestly, you face consequences. The idea is one of cause and effect, karma, and fairness.
It Works for Both Good and Bad Outcomes

This is crucial. "Reap" is neutral — it does not tell you whether the result is positive or negative. The object of the verb tells you that.

Positive examples:

  • "After years of studying, she began to reap the rewards of her effort."
  • "The company reaped enormous profits from its new product."
  • "He reaped the benefits of eating healthy — more energy, better sleep."

Negative examples:

  • "He reaped the consequences of his years of neglect."
  • "Those who spread lies will eventually reap the results of their actions."
  • "The corrupt official reaped what he had sown — disgrace and punishment."
The Feel and Tone of the Word

"Reap" carries a slightly weighty, serious tone. It implies that the result wasn't accidental — it was earned or brought upon oneself. When used in the negative sense, it often sounds like a form of justice being served. When used positively, it sounds like well-deserved success.

You wouldn't typically say "I reaped a nice lunch today." That sounds odd because "reap" implies effort, time, and a meaningful consequence — not a casual, small event. It's a word suited to significant outcomes that follow significant actions.

The verb is almost always followed by something you receive:

  • Reap the rewards — the most common phrase
  • Reap the benefits
  • Reap the profits / gains
  • Reap the fruits (of your labor)
  • Reap the consequences / punishment
  • Reap the harvest (literal or figurative)
  • Reap what you sow (the classic phrase)

You'll notice these are all results or outcomes, not actions. You don't "reap a decision" or "reap a plan." You reap what comes out of those decisions and plans.

In its literal sense, reaping refers to the physical act of cutting standing crops close to the ground — traditionally done with a curved blade called a sickle, and today done with machines called combine harvesters. This is a harvest activity: the crops grow over months, and at exactly the right moment of ripeness, farmers reap them before they spoil or fall.

This literal image is exactly why the figurative meaning works so well: the gap between effort and reward (you plant, you wait, then you harvest) maps perfectly onto real life.

LiteralTo cut and gather a crop at harvest time
FigurativeTo receive the results — good or bad — of your own actions
Key feelDeserved outcome; cause and effect; significant consequence
ToneSerious, weighty; not casual
Most famous use"You reap what you sow"
One Final Way to Remember It

Think of it this way: reaping is the moment of collection after a long process. Whether it's a farmer collecting crops or a student collecting a degree after years of studying, or a dishonest person finally facing the results of their behavior — reaping is when you receive what was always coming to you. It's the universe settling the account.
13375: To understand "reaper," you first need to understand one simple action: reaping. Reaping means cutting down crops — like wheat, barley, or rice — when they are fully grown and ready to be collected. This process is called the harvest. A reaper, then, is something or someone that does this cutting.
Meaning 1: A person who cuts crops (the original, literal meaning)

Hundreds of years ago, before machines existed, harvesting was done entirely by hand. Farmers and workers would walk through fields and use a tool called a scythe — a long handle with a large, curved, razor-sharp blade at the bottom — to slice through the stalks of grain close to the ground. The person doing this physically demanding work was called a reaper.

This was one of the most important jobs in farming societies. If the crop wasn't harvested in time, it would rot or be destroyed by weather, and people would have nothing to eat through winter. Reapers were essential to survival.

"The reapers worked from sunrise to sunset to bring in the wheat before the rains came."
Meaning 2: A machine that cuts crops

When machinery arrived in the 1800s, engineers built mechanical devices that could cut crops far faster than any human. These machines were also called reapers, because they performed the exact same job. Later, more advanced machines combined reaping with other steps (like separating the grain from the stalk) and became known as "combine harvesters." But the earlier, simpler cutting machines were simply called reapers.

"The mechanical reaper changed farming forever, allowing one farmer to do the work of an entire crew."
Meaning 3: The Grim Reaper — Death itself (the most famous and widely used meaning today)

This is where the word becomes far larger than farming.

Over many centuries, people began to notice a powerful similarity between the way a reaper harvests crops and the way Death takes human lives. From this comparison was born one of the most enduring and widely recognized symbols in human culture: the Grim Reaper.

The Grim Reaper is what's known as a personification of Death — meaning Death is imagined and depicted not as an abstract concept, but as an actual figure you can picture. That figure is almost always shown as:

  • A tall, dark, hooded skeleton (or a shadowy, robed figure whose face cannot be seen)
  • Carrying a long scythe — the same tool used to cut grain
  • Silent, patient, and unstoppable

The scythe is the crucial detail here. It directly links the act of harvesting crops to the idea of Death "harvesting" human lives. Just as a reaper cuts down wheat stalks in a field, the Grim Reaper is imagined to "cut down" human beings when their time comes.

The word "Grim" means harsh, merciless, and without warmth — which fits perfectly with how people imagine Death.

"In the painting, the Grim Reaper stood silently at the soldier's bedside, scythe in hand."

"People jokingly said the old car was so dangerous, driving it was an appointment with the Grim Reaper."
Why the comparison between Death and a reaper is so powerful

The metaphor works on multiple levels, and understanding why makes the word much richer:

  • Crops grow, mature, and must eventually be cut down — just as humans are born, live, and eventually die.
  • A harvest can sweep through an entire field at once — just as war, famine, or disease can take thousands of lives at once.
  • A reaper does not choose which individual stalks to spare and which to cut — Death is seen as equally indifferent to who it takes.
  • The harvest cannot be stopped or postponed indefinitely — just as death is seen as inevitable for every living thing.

This metaphor was so fitting and so vivid that it has lasted for thousands of years and remains in active use in literature, art, film, and everyday speech today.

Because of the Grim Reaper symbol, the word "reaper" by itself — even without the word "Grim" in front of it — often carries a dark, death-related tone. In writing, fiction, poetry, and conversation, when someone uses the word "reaper" alone, they are usually hinting at or directly referring to Death.

"He had cheated the reaper for the third time in his life."

(Meaning: he had narrowly escaped death three times.)

"The reaper comes for all of us eventually."

(Meaning: death is inevitable for everyone.)
"Reaper" in the famous proverb: You reap what you sow

This proverb uses the agricultural meaning of the word to teach a moral lesson. "Sow" means to plant seeds. "Reap" means to harvest what grew from those seeds.

The saying means: whatever you put into your actions — good or bad — is what you will eventually receive in return. If you plant good seeds through hard work, honesty, and kindness, your harvest (the result of your life) will be good. If you plant bad seeds through dishonesty or cruelty, your harvest will reflect that too.

In this context, a reaper is simply someone collecting the results of their own past choices — which is why the word sometimes carries a sense of karma or justice.

"He treated everyone around him badly for years. Now, struggling and alone, he was reaping what he had sown."

A reaper is a cutter of crops — a person or machine that harvests grain. But because Death was imagined as something that "harvests" human lives in the same way, the word grew into a symbol of Death itself. Today, the Grim Reaper is one of the most universally recognized images in the world, and the word "reaper" carries that weight even when used alone.

Whether you encounter it in a history book about farming, a painting of Death, a fantasy novel, a poem about mortality, or a proverb about consequences — you now know exactly what it means and where that meaning comes from.
13376:
To reappraise something means to look at it again carefully and form a fresh judgment about it — especially after some time has passed, new information has come in, or circumstances have changed.

Think of it in two parts:

  • Appraise = to carefully study something and decide what you think of it — its value, quality, importance, or meaning.
  • Re- = to do that same thing again.

So to reappraise is to go back and ask yourself: "Now that I know what I know, do I still think the same thing about this?"
What Makes It Different From Just "Thinking Again"

This is important. Reappraising is not the same as casually reconsidering something for a moment. It carries a sense of:

  • Deliberate effort — you are consciously sitting down to evaluate something with fresh eyes.
  • A previous judgment already existing — you already had a view, and now you're re-examining it.
  • A meaningful reason to revisit — something prompted the re-evaluation: new evidence, a major life event, the passing of time, a failure, a success, or simply gaining maturity and wisdom.

The word carries a slightly formal, serious tone. It suggests that the act of looking again is thorough and meaningful, not just a passing second thought.

Example 1 — A person:
You once thought a colleague was lazy. But after working closely with them for a year, you discover they were dealing with a serious personal crisis. You now reappraise them — and realize they are actually resilient and dedicated.

Example 2 — A decision:
A government introduces a new tax policy. After seeing that it is hurting small businesses, officials reappraise the policy and decide to make changes.

Example 3 — Art or literature:
A film was considered a failure when it was released. Years later, critics watch it again with fresh perspective and reappraise it as ahead of its time.

Example 4 — A personal belief:
You grew up believing that success means earning a lot of money. After a difficult experience, you reappraise that belief and decide that success actually means having time for the people you love.

Example 5 — A relationship:
After an argument with a close friend, you sit quietly and reappraise the friendship — weighing the good years against the current conflict — and decide it's worth saving.

Almost anything that can be judged can be reappraised. Common things people reappraise include:

  • A person (their character, intentions, or ability)
  • A decision or policy
  • A belief or value
  • A relationship
  • A piece of work (art, writing, music, architecture)
  • A situation or crisis
  • Oneself (your own choices, behavior, or identity)

This is a subtle but important point. When you reappraise something, the conclusion is open. You might:

  • Change your view completely — you realize you were wrong before.
  • Partially revise your view — you refine and adjust what you thought.
  • Confirm your original view — you look again and decide you were right all along. (This still counts as reappraising — the process happened, even if the outcome stayed the same.)

The word doesn't promise a change. It promises a genuine re-examination.

Reappraise is a moderately formal word. You'll find it in:

  • News articles and journalism
  • Academic and professional writing
  • Thoughtful personal reflection
  • Political and policy discussions

In casual conversation, people might say "take another look at," "rethink," or "reconsider" instead. But reappraise carries a slightly more rigorous, considered weight than those alternatives.

• Reappraisal (noun) — the act of reappraising. "The reappraisal of his legacy took decades."
  • Appraise (verb) — the first-time version of the act, without the "re-."
  • Reconsider — similar, but lighter; to reconsider is to think again, while to reappraise is to evaluate again in a deeper, more structured sense.
  • Reassess — nearly identical in meaning; often interchangeable with reappraise. Both mean to evaluate again. Reassess feels slightly more analytical or systematic; reappraise slightly more qualitative and judgmental in the neutral sense.
  • Review — broader and more routine; a review can be a first look or a repeated one, while reappraise always implies going back.
The Single-Sentence Definition You Can Always Return To

To reappraise is to deliberately and carefully evaluate something again — a person, idea, work, decision, or belief — in light of new information, changed circumstances, or simply a wiser perspective, in order to arrive at a fresh and honest judgment.
13377:
To understand reappraised, you first need to understand its root word.

To appraise something means to carefully look at it, study it, and form a judgment about its value, quality, or importance. Think of it like giving something an official verdict after thinking it through.

Now, the prefix re- simply means again or anew.

So, to reappraise means to judge or evaluate something a second time — usually because something has changed: new information appeared, time passed, or the first judgment turned out to be incomplete or wrong.

Reappraised, in its adjective form, describes something that has already gone through this second evaluation. It is used to describe the subject — the thing, person, idea, or work — that was looked at again and given a fresh verdict.
Breaking It Down With a Simple Image

Imagine you're a judge at a fruit market. You look at a basket of apples and declare, "These are ordinary apples. Three stars." That's an appraisal.

A week later, someone tells you these apples are actually a rare variety grown only in one valley in the world. You study them again, taste them again, and now you declare, "These are extraordinary. Five stars."

Those apples are now reappraised apples — they are the same apples, but they carry a new, revised judgment after being looked at again.

When you call something reappraised, you are silently communicating several things at once:

  1. A first judgment existed. Something was already evaluated before.
  2. That first judgment has been revisited. Someone looked at it again, more carefully or with fresh eyes.
  3. A new, often different conclusion has been reached. The outcome of this second look may confirm, upgrade, downgrade, or completely overturn the original verdict.
  4. The subject is now seen in a new light. The reappraised thing stands in a different position in people's understanding or estimation.

This is an important point: reappraised does not simply mean "evaluated." It specifically signals that a change in perspective or judgment has occurred after a previous one. If there was no first appraisal, there can be no reappraisal.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

Reappraised is used across many areas of life. Here are the most common ones:

Art and Literature
A novel that was ignored when first published but is later recognized as a masterpiece is called a reappraised work. The book itself didn't change. What changed is how people understand and value it now compared to before.

"The reappraised novel is now considered one of the greatest of its century."

History and Historical Figures
People from the past are often reappraised as new documents are discovered or as society's values evolve. A leader once celebrated as a hero might, after historians dig deeper, be reappraised as a more complicated or even troubling figure — and vice versa.

"The reappraised general is now seen as both a military genius and a deeply flawed human being."

Property and Finance
A house, a piece of land, or a company can be reappraised when market conditions change or when new information (like structural damage or a nearby new development) changes its worth.

"The reappraised property sold for twice its original estimated value."

Scientific and Medical Ideas
A theory that was once accepted, then rejected, and then proven to be correct after all, can be described as reappraised.

"The reappraised findings from the 1970s study are now considered groundbreaking."

Personal Beliefs and Relationships
Even in everyday life, a person's character, a past decision, or a belief system can be reappraised. Someone you once thought was dishonest, but later understood was acting under pressure, is a reappraised person in your mind.

Reappraised is not a neutral word. It carries a quiet sense of correction, maturity, and open-mindedness. When something is described as reappraised, it signals that people were willing to set aside their first impressions and look again — which takes intellectual honesty.

It can also carry a sense of justice, especially when someone or something was unfairly dismissed the first time and is now being given the recognition it deserves.

Occasionally, it goes the other direction — something once praised is reappraised and found wanting. In that case, the word carries a note of disillusionment or revision downward.
How It Sits in a Sentence

As an adjective, reappraised always describes a noun — the thing that has been evaluated again:

  • "The reappraised manuscript revealed a far more complex author than anyone had suspected."
  • "After decades of neglect, the reappraised paintings are finally receiving the attention they deserve."
  • "The reappraised evidence changed the entire direction of the investigation."
  • "She was a reappraised figure in feminist scholarship — once sidelined, now central."
Synonyms That Help You Anchor the Meaning

If you ever need a simpler word in place of reappraised, these work similarly:

  • Re-evaluated — looked at again and judged anew
  • Reassessed — measured or examined again
  • Reconsidered — thought about again with fresh perspective
  • Revised — (in terms of judgment) changed after review
  • Rehabilitated — (specifically when someone's reputation improves after being reconsidered)

None of these are perfect replacements — each has its own shade — but they all share the central idea of a second, fresh look resulting in a new judgment.

If you had to define it in one sentence:

Reappraised describes something that has been examined and judged a second time — usually resulting in a new or updated understanding of its value, quality, or importance.

That's the word in full. It's a small word doing big work: it tells you that something has a history of being judged, that judgment has been revisited, and that the subject now stands in a new light because of it.
13378:
When you say something is reasoned, you mean it is based on careful, logical thinking — not on gut feeling, emotion, or guesswork. A reasoned idea, argument, or decision has been thought through deliberately and methodically, with evidence and logic supporting it.

Think of it this way: if you arrive at a conclusion by actually working through the problem step by step, weighing the evidence, and building a logical case — that conclusion is reasoned. If you just blurt out whatever feels right in the moment, it is not.

The word carries a few important qualities at once:

1. It was arrived at through a process, not an accident.
A reasoned argument didn't just appear. Someone thought it through, examined the facts, and built up to a conclusion in an organized way.

2. It is supported, not bare.
A reasoned view doesn't stand alone as a naked opinion. It comes with backing — logic, evidence, clear explanation, or sound argument. You can look at the reasoning and evaluate it.

3. It is deliberate, not impulsive.
A reasoned response is the opposite of a knee-jerk reaction. The person paused, thought, and then spoke or decided.

4. It implies quality, not just effort.
"Reasoned" has a positive connotation. It suggests that the thinking was done well — that the logic actually holds up. Simply rambling through disorganized thoughts would not usually be called "reasoned."
Common Expressions Where You'll See It

• A reasoned argument — an argument built logically, step by step, with supporting points
  • A reasoned decision — a decision made after carefully thinking through the options and their consequences
  • A reasoned explanation — an explanation that makes its logic clear and follows a coherent structure
  • A reasoned opinion — an opinion that is backed by thought and evidence, not just personal taste
  • A reasoned debate — a debate conducted with logic and evidence rather than emotion or personal attacks
  • A reasoned approach — a method of doing something that is thoughtful, systematic, and justified

Understanding what "reasoned" contrasts with will sharpen your understanding:

Opposite typeWhat it means
EmotionalDriven by feelings rather than logic
ImpulsiveDone without thinking first
ArbitraryBased on no real logic or principle
InstinctiveBased on gut feeling, not worked-out thought
IrrationalContradicts logic or evidence

In short: anything unreflective, gut-driven, or poorly supported is the opposite of "reasoned."
Real-Life Examples to Lock It In

Example 1:

"The judge gave a reasoned ruling that cited three legal precedents and explained why each applied to this case."

Here, the ruling wasn't just "guilty" or "not guilty" with no explanation. It was backed by clear, step-by-step legal logic.

Example 2:

"She gave a reasoned explanation for why the company should invest in renewable energy — she presented data on cost savings, environmental impact, and long-term risk."

Her explanation wasn't just a vague feeling that renewables are good. It was structured, supported, and logical.

Example 3:

"His reasoned response to the criticism showed he had genuinely thought about the issue rather than reacting defensively."

Instead of snapping back emotionally, he calmly laid out a logical reply — that is what made it "reasoned."

Example 4 (showing contrast):

"She rejected the proposal not with any reasoned argument, but purely out of personal dislike."

The absence of reasoning is the point here — she had no logic, only feeling.

These words are easy to confuse, so here is how they differ:

Reasoned vs. Rational:
"Rational" describes a quality — it means in accordance with reason or sensible. A person can be rational; a system can be rational. "Reasoned," by contrast, specifically emphasizes that the process of reasoning was carried out — that someone actually did the thinking work. A reasoned argument is one where you can see the reasoning laid out. A rational argument is one that makes logical sense.

Reasoned vs. Reasonable:
"Reasonable" means fair, sensible, and within the bounds of common sense — it is a softer, more everyday word. You might say a price is reasonable, or that a request is reasonable. "Reasoned" is more specific and more rigorous — it means built on explicit reasoning and argument, not just sensible in a general way.

Reasoned vs. Logical:
"Logical" means following correctly from premises — it is about the structure of the argument. "Reasoned" includes that, but implies something more: a fuller, deliberate effort to work through a problem, present a case, and support a conclusion. All reasoned arguments are logical, but not everything called logical necessarily represents a full, deliberate reasoning process.
"Reasoned" means carefully thought through, logically supported, and deliberately argued — the opposite of emotional, impulsive, or arbitrary.
13379:
To reassure someone means to say or do something that removes their worry, fear, or doubt, and makes them feel calm, safe, or confident again.

Think of it this way: someone is feeling unsettled inside — nervous, scared, or uncertain. You step in and do or say something that settles them back down. That act of settling them is reassuring them.
The "Before" State: Why Reassurance Is Needed

Reassurance is only needed when something has gone wrong in someone's mind — when they are experiencing one of these:

  • Fear — "What if something bad happens?"
  • Doubt — "I'm not sure this is okay."
  • Worry — "I keep thinking about what could go wrong."
  • Insecurity — "Maybe I'm not good enough."
  • Uncertainty — "I don't know what's going to happen."

Without this troubled state of mind, there is nothing to reassure. This is an important part of the word's meaning — it always implies that someone was unsettled before the reassurance happened.
What You Actually Do When You Reassure Someone

Reassuring someone is not one fixed action. You can reassure through many different means:

  • Words — Telling someone that things are fine, that they have nothing to fear, or that the outcome will be good. "Everything is going to be okay," a mother tells her child.
  • Information or facts — Giving someone evidence or explanation that removes their fear. A doctor shows a patient their test results and explains that the numbers are completely normal.
  • Your presence or manner — Simply being calm and steady can reassure someone. A flight attendant's relaxed smile during mild turbulence reassures nervous passengers without saying a word.
  • Actions — Doing something that proves things are safe. A mechanic takes a car for a test drive in front of the worried owner to show it is working perfectly.

The key is that whatever you do must reach the other person's inner fear or doubt and dissolve it (or at least reduce it).

This is important: not only people can reassure.

  • A person can reassure another person. "Her friend reassured her that she looked wonderful."
  • You can reassure yourself. "He kept reassuring himself that he had studied enough." (This is called reflexive use.)
  • A thing, event, or piece of information can reassure someone. "The strong safety test results reassured the engineers." Here, the results themselves — not a person — are doing the reassuring.
  • A tone, look, or gesture can reassure. "His calm voice reassured the crowd."

After being reassured, the person typically feels:

  • Calmer
  • More confident
  • Less afraid
  • Relieved
  • At ease
  • More certain

They still know the problem or the uncertainty exists — but they no longer feel threatened or overwhelmed by it. Their emotional weight is lifted.

These examples show the word used in a variety of ways, so you can see how naturally it fits different situations:

  1. The nurse reassured the frightened child that the injection would only hurt for a moment.
  2. My manager reassured me that my job was not at risk despite the company's losses.
  3. She kept reassuring herself that she had made the right decision.
  4. His confident handshake and steady gaze reassured the client immediately.
  5. The clear weather forecast reassured the farmers who had been worried about their harvest.
  6. No matter how many times they reassured him, he remained nervous before the exam.
  7. The pilot's calm announcement reassured the passengers during the storm.

1. Reassurance does not guarantee truth.
When you reassure someone, you are trying to remove their fear — but what you say may or may not be true. A parent might say, "Don't worry, you'll do great!" before a performance without actually knowing how it will go. The intent is to comfort. Whether it turns out to be accurate is a separate matter.

However, in serious, responsible contexts (medicine, law, safety), reassurance is expected to be honest and accurate — a doctor should only reassure a patient if the situation genuinely warrants it.

2. Reassurance can fail.
You can attempt to reassure someone and fail. "I tried to reassure her, but she was still terrified." The action of reassuring requires that the other person actually receives and accepts the comfort. If they don't, the reassurance didn't "land."

3. Repeated reassurance can be a sign of deep anxiety.
If someone constantly needs reassurance about the same thing again and again, it often signals that they are genuinely struggling with anxiety. Each reassurance gives them only temporary relief. This is a nuance the word carries in psychological contexts.

4. Reassuring can be sincere or hollow.
"He said the words to reassure her, but he didn't believe them himself." Reassurance can be offered genuinely or merely as a social act to soothe someone — even if the speaker has doubts.

These words are close in meaning but not interchangeable:

Comfort — More general. You comfort someone who is sad, grieving, or in pain. It doesn't necessarily target a specific fear or doubt. You can comfort someone who just lost a loved one — not to remove their grief, but to be with them in it. Reassuring is more targeted: it specifically aims to remove or reduce a doubt or fear.

Console — Used when someone has already experienced a loss or setback. You console someone after their team loses, after a relationship ends, after a disappointment. Reassuring usually happens before or during the feared event, trying to prevent the fear from growing.

Encourage — To encourage is to give someone motivation and confidence to take action. "Go on, you can do it!" Reassuring is about removing a fear that is already there. The two sometimes overlap, but encouraging is more forward-pushing while reassuring is more fear-dissolving.

Promise — A promise is a specific commitment about a future outcome. Reassuring doesn't require a promise. You can reassure someone through tone, facts, presence, or explanation — without committing to any outcome.

All of these come from the same root and you will encounter them often:

  • Reassure (verb) — the action: "Let me reassure you."
  • Reassured (past tense / adjective) — describes the state after: "She felt reassured after the conversation."
  • Reassuring (adjective / present participle) — describes something that gives reassurance: "He had a reassuring smile." / "He is reassuring the patient right now."
  • Reassurance (noun) — the act or feeling itself: "She needed reassurance that she was loved."
  • Reassuringly (adverb) — in a way that reassures: "He spoke reassuringly."
One-Line Summary to Anchor It All
To reassure is to say, show, or do something that calms another person's fear, doubt, or worry — making them feel safe, confident, or at ease again.
